lead: You forecast for yourself here: chart, barometer and sky first, then the official forecast weighed against the coast.

sections.title: Isobars and the barometer

qa.q: With my back to the wind, where is the area of low pressure?
qa.a: On your left and a little ahead, in the northern hemisphere: **Buys Ballot's law**. Wind blows anticlockwise round a low and clockwise round a high, angled slightly towards the low pressure.

refs: Pressure systems — wind round a low
Pressure systems — wind round a high

blocks.p: In the north, wind blows anticlockwise round a low and clockwise round a high, angled slightly towards low pressure. Back to the wind, the low is on your left, a little ahead: **Buys Ballot's law**.
Halve the isobar spacing and the wind doubles. The chart's **geostrophic scale** reads the wind aloft: at sea take two thirds, more at lower latitudes for the same spacing.
A fast rise blows as hard as a fast fall; an offset error leaves the tendency true.

sections.title: What a passing low does

qa.q: Will the wind veer or back as a depression passes?
qa.a: If the centre passes north of you the wind **veers**, clockwise through S, SW and NW; if it passes south, it **backs** through SE, E and NE. A frontal low travels along its warm-sector isobars.

refs: Depressions — the track of the centre
Reading a synoptic chart — movement of a low
Reading a synoptic chart — a 48 h plan

blocks.p: A frontal low travels along its **warm-sector** isobars. If the centre passes north of you the wind **veers**, clockwise: S, SW, NW. If it passes south, the wind **backs**: SE, E, NE.

fig.note: North of you, moving E: veers

blocks.p: When the cold front catches the warm one the low is **occluded**: it stops deepening and fills. An occlusion brings rain, then a veer and showers. A **trough** is a weak front; a **ridge** between lows a brief fair spell, so sail early. A **secondary low** on the trailing front can deepen fast and outblow its parent.

sections.title: Sources, words and limits

qa.q: What does "gale soon" mean in a forecast?
qa.a: **Soon** means 6 to 12 hours from the time of issue; imminent is within 6 hours, later over 12. A gale warning for soon, issued at 0600 UTC, means any time from 1200 to 1800 UTC.

refs: GRIB files vs the official forecast
GRIB files — age of the forecast

blocks.p: **NAVTEX**: English on 518 kHz, national language on 490; types A, B and D (navigational and weather warnings, search and rescue) cannot be switched off. A SÉCURITÉ call on VHF 16 names a working channel: go there and write it down.

fig.title: Gale warning, issued 0600 UTC
lines: So: any time from 1200 to 1800 UTC

blocks.p: A **GRIB** is one model's mean wind on a coarse grid: no gusts, no funnelling. Add the coast yourself, plan on the earlier of two models, trust the newest official forecast. A barb points where the wind comes from: long feather 10 kn, short 5.

sections.title: Beaufort, apparent wind, waves

qa.q: Why is the sea so steep off a headland when the wind is against the tide?
qa.a: **Wind against tide** makes short, steep, breaking seas, worst off headlands at full stream. Round them near slack water and well off, and avoid shoal banks, where seas break as the depth falls to about their height.

refs: Beaufort — the true wind at night
Sea state — swell and wind sea
Wind against tide — timing at a headland
Local winds — the sea they raise

blocks.p: Beaufort force is the **mean** wind (force 7: 28–33 kn); log gusts beside it. Rig load grows as the square of the wind: 24 kn pulls 2¼ times as hard as 16.

Waves grow with wind, **fetch** and duration: the least sea lies under a weather shore. Forecast heights are **significant**: the odd wave is nearly twice as high. Swell and wind sea combine as √(swell² + sea²): 2.0 and 1.5 m give 2.5 m. A new long swell announces a distant low.

fig.note: W wind over a W-going stream: steep, breaking at A

blocks.p: **Wind against tide** makes short, steep, breaking seas, worst off headlands at full stream: round near slack water, well off. Seas also break where depth falls to about their height: avoid shoal banks.

sections.title: Breezes and high land

qa.q: When does the sea breeze start and how strong does it get?
qa.a: On a settled day a **sea breeze** sets in by late morning, reaches force 3–4 by mid-afternoon, veers a little and dies at dusk. A light offshore wind can hold it off behind a calm belt.

refs: Sea breeze — against an offshore wind
Local effects — lee of a high island

blocks.p: On a settled day a **sea breeze** sets in by late morning, reaches force 3–4 by mid-afternoon, veers a little and dies at dusk; hot slopes strengthen it (**anabatic**). A light offshore wind holds it off behind a calm belt. By night a **land breeze** blows, and off steep slopes a cold **katabatic** wind, strongest before dawn.

High land bends the wind along straits and round headlands, and speeds it up. A high island casts a **wind shadow** with a sharp edge, yet in strong winds gusts fall down its lee slopes, hardest at night. Lens-shaped clouds over the peaks warn of them.

qa.q: When is the best time to sail upwind in the Meltemi?
qa.a: At dawn, before it builds: the **Meltemi** blows from the north in the Aegean, under clear skies, at force 6–7 for days, peaking after noon, set up by a Balkan high and a Turkish low.

blocks.p: Make upwind miles at dawn, before a Meltemi builds. Gusts in km/h ÷ 1.852 give knots: 100 km/h is 54 kn.

sections.title: No visibility, sudden wind

qa.q: Will a stronger wind clear sea fog?
qa.a: No: **sea fog** is warm moist air over colder water, and wind does not clear it; a sea breeze carries it inshore. Radiation fog, formed over land on clear calm nights, is gone by mid-morning.

refs: Fog — sea fog and the sea breeze

blocks.p: Fog forms as air cools to its **dew point**: a degree apart, fix your position, ready radar and horn. **Sea fog** is warm moist air over colder water: wind does not clear it; a sea breeze carries it inshore. **Radiation fog** forms over land on clear calm nights, gone by mid-morning. **Frontal fog** lifts once the warm front passes.

fig.note: Sea temperatures · fog from C on, below the dew point

blocks.p: A **thunderstorm** throws a cold gust front ahead of its rain: reef first; at anchor, leave room to swing right round. Over high ground they break late in the day. Flash-to-thunder seconds ÷ 3 give kilometres. Stars vanishing to windward: a squall. After a strike, check the through-hulls and hull for leaks first.
